food.text: Around 1370 BCE, a teenage girl was buried in an oak coffin at Egtved, Denmark. Beside her stood a birch bark container of fermented drink made from wheat, honey, bog-myrtle and cowberries, laid with flowering yarrow.

The Funnelbeaker culture, which lasted until about 2800 BCE, introduced farming and husbandry as major food sources to pottery-using hunter-gatherers. Its northern group covered northern Germany and southern Scandinavia.

The Pitted Ware culture (c. 3500 BC to c. 2300 BC) lived along the coasts of southern Scandinavia. Its economy was based on fishing, hunting and gathering plants, even though farming had already reached the region.

Crop analyses from northern Germany, Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands show Funnelbeaker sites dominated by naked barley and emmer. Einkorn and free-threshing wheat also turned up frequently, though only in small quantities.
The Funnelbeaker culture was dominated by animal husbandry of sheep, cattle, pigs and goats. Hunting and fishing still added to the food supply.
Hunting seal was particularly important to the Pitted Ware people of southern Scandinavia. Because of this, they have been called "hard-core sealers" or the "Inuit of the Baltic".
Pitted Ware sites contain bones from elk, deer, beaver, seal, porpoise and pig. The large quantities of pig bones on some sites come from wild boar rather than domestic pigs.
Hard or rivet wheat has been demonstrated at Frydenlund and in Albersdorf. It is an uncommon find among the Funnelbeaker crops, which were dominated by naked barley and emmer.

art.text: Lurs are giant curving Bronze Age horns, normally made of bronze and often decorated. Of the 53 known examples, 35 have been found in bogs in Denmark, very often in pairs.

Scandinavian rock art made by farmers, usually in the Nordic Bronze Age, shows cup marks, boats, horses, people brandishing weapons, foot soles, wagons and abstract symbols such as spirals and concentric circles. It is a very different world from the hunted animals of earlier Stone Age carvings.
The Trundholm sun chariot is a significant artifact from the 2nd millennium BC. It is counted as part of the art of the Nordic Bronze Age, a tradition that later gave way to Norse and Viking art.
Central Norway contains approximately 300 rock carving and rock painting sites from the Stone Age and Bronze Age. Petroglyph sites are much more plentiful there than rock painting sites.

Danish archaeologist Flemming Kaul studied illustrations on Danish bronze items to try to recreate a complete Bronze Age cosmology. He suggests the horse pulled the sun across the sky by day, and the boat carried it back through the underworld at night.

Cheek-pieces and whip handles found in Denmark from around 1700 BC carry curvilinear 'wave-band' designs. The same designs appear on contemporary artefacts from the Carpathian Basin and Greece, including the elite shaft graves at Mycenae.

The Nordic Bronze Age maintained close trade links with Mycenaean Greece, with whom it shares several striking similarities. Copper was imported from Britain in the Early Bronze Age in exchange for amber.
The wave-band designs first seen on Danish cheek-pieces and whip handles later appear on Nordic Bronze Age metalwork. One of the places they appear is the gold disc of the Trundholm Sun Chariot.
Engraved depictions of chariots appear in Scandinavian rock art from about 1700 BC onwards. They also appear on engraved stone stelae from Mycenae, showing a shared image across distant lands.

Cheek-pieces and whip handles in Denmark from about 1700 BC feature curvilinear wave-band designs also found on contemporary artefacts from Greece, including in the elite shaft graves at Mycenae. The designs later appear on Nordic metalwork such as the gold disc of the Trundholm Sun Chariot. Engraved chariots appear on stone stelae from Mycenae.

Cheek-pieces and belt hooks adorned with horse heads are suggested to have originated from the Carpathian Basin, and to have made their way into Scandinavia. They show how decorative motifs travelled along with new horse technology.

war.text: The Battle Axe culture, also called the Boat Axe culture, flourished in the coastal areas of southern Scandinavia and southwest Finland from about 2800 BC to 2300 BC. It replaced the Funnelbeaker culture in southern Scandinavia, probably through mass migration and population replacement.

Towards the end of the 3rd millennium BC, the people of southern Scandinavia were overrun by new groups, the Battle-Axe culture. They advanced up to Uppland and the Oslofjord. This culture had the battle axe as a status symbol, and its people were cattle herders.
Swords from the Nordic Bronze Age appear from about the 17th century BC, and they often show characteristic spiral patterns. The early Nordic swords were comparatively short.
Rock carvings at Tanum in Bohuslän, Sweden, show humans holding a bow, spear or axe. The carvings are a World Heritage Site because so many are found together.

In Central Norway, Bronze Age farmers carved rock art showing boats, horses and people, often brandishing weapons. Nearly all of the roughly 300 carving and painting sites in the region date to the Stone Age and Bronze Age.

A sword found in 1912 near Bragby, Uppland, Sweden, dates to about 1800 to 1500 BC and is just over 60 cm long. It belongs to the Hajdúsámson-Apa type, so it was presumably imported rather than made locally.
Defensive palisades were built in Funnelbeaker territory in the early 3rd millennium BCE. They may be a sign of violent conflict between the Funnelbeakers, Corded Ware and Pitted Ware peoples.
The Vreta Kloster sword, found in 1897 and dated to 1600 to 1500 BC, has a blade length of only 46 cm. Its hilt is missing, which shows how short some early Nordic swords were.

literature.text: Northern Europe entered the protohistorical period only in the early centuries AD, with the adoption of writing and ethnographic accounts by Roman authors. Before that, the Nordic Bronze Age left no written literature, and its story is told through objects and images.

In Norse mythology the sun goddess Sól travels across the sky in a horse-drawn wagon. This motif dates to the Nordic Bronze Age, as shown on the Trundholm sun chariot. A story pictured in bronze thus seems to have lasted into much later Old Norse literature.

Sól appears in the Poetic Edda, compiled in the 13th century from earlier traditional sources, and in Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda. Both call her the sister of the moon, Máni, and foretell that a monstrous wolf will kill her during Ragnarök, though she will first give birth to a daughter who continues her course. In the Prose Edda, the wolf Sköll chases her across the sky, so close behind that she has no escape except to run, and despite her fear he will eventually catch her.

Scholar John Lindow says the Sun seems to have been a focus of older Scandinavian religious practices. Yet he finds it difficult to argue for a central role for the sun in the surviving sources for Norse mythology. He also suggests Sól is female and Máni male because of the grammatical gender of the nouns.

science.text: Southern Scandinavia became the richest bronze-working culture in Europe. During the 15th and 14th centuries BC, it produced and deposited more elaborate bronzes in graves and hoards than any other European region. Judged by the number and density of metal deposits, the Nordic Bronze Age was the richest culture in Europe.

Bronze tools arrived in Scandinavia shortly after 2000 BC. From 1750 BC the region adopted bronze metalworking technology more systematically. The metallurgical influences were especially noticeable from Central Europe, and were tied to people similar to those of the Únětice culture.

Scandinavians were making metal before the Bronze Age began. The Bell Beaker culture in Jutland, Denmark, practised copper metallurgy from about 2400 BC, including the production of axes and ornaments. Bronze followed only later.
Denmark has yielded more Bronze Age swords than anywhere else in Europe. Uniform crucibles found at metal workshop sites suggest that certain metal artefacts were mass produced.

Britain was the first region in Europe to fully adopt tin-bronze, switching all its metalwork to it in 2200 to 2100 BC. Scandinavia and Central Europe made the same full switch by around 1800 BC. Southern Iberia, the Aegean and Egypt followed later, around 1500 to 1300 BC.

Around 2800 BC, metal was introduced in Scandinavia in the Corded Ware culture. In much of Scandinavia, a Battle Axe culture then became prominent, known from some 3,000 graves. Towards the end of the 3rd millennium BC, these newcomers overran the Funnelbeaker people, and many scholars think they spoke Proto-Indo-European.

Around 2100 BCE, Scandinavia's metal production and exchange increased, with copper imported from Slovakia via central Germany and tin from the British Isles. Later, in the Early Bronze Age, copper was also imported from Britain in exchange for amber.
Some of the earliest bronze artefacts in Scandinavia come from hoards at Pile in Sweden and Skeldal in Denmark. They date from about 2000 to 1700 BC.

Scandinavia could not make its own bronze, because tin was not a local natural resource. This dependence on distant supplies shaped the region's bronze culture. Later, new techniques let iron production from bog iron, mostly in Denmark, slowly gain ground.

A genetic study published in Nature in June 2015 examined a Battle Axe male buried in Viby, Sweden, around 2621 to 2472 BC. He carried the paternal haplogroup R1a1a1, and Scandinavian people of this time were found to be closely related to those of the Corded Ware culture.

Two Battle Axe individuals buried in Bergsgraven in central Sweden were mostly of Western Steppe Herder descent, with slight Western Hunter-Gatherer and Early European Farmer admixture. The admixture appears to have come from the mating of Western Steppe Herder males with Early European Farmer and Western Hunter-Gatherer females. Western Steppe Herder ancestry had not been detected among earlier local populations, which supported the idea that the Battle Axe culture emerged from migrations from southeast of the Baltic.

politics.text: From about 2,800 BC, the hunter-gatherers of the Pitted Ware culture shared southern Scandinavia with Corded Ware peoples such as the Battle Axe culture. The Corded Ware built defensive palisades, which may be a sign of violent conflict with the Pitted Ware. By about 2,300 BC the Pitted Ware culture had merged into the Battle Axe culture.

The Battle Axe culture replaced the Funnelbeaker culture in southern Scandinavia from about 2800 BC, probably through mass migration and population replacement. It later absorbed the Pitted Ware culture and developed into the Nordic Bronze Age.

The Nordic Bronze Age kept close trade links with Mycenaean Greece, with which it shares several striking similarities. Around 2100 BCE, a network of exchange brought copper from Slovakia via central Germany, and tin from the British Isles, to the north.

Genetic study of Battle Axe burials at Bergsgraven in central Sweden found ancestry markedly different from that of earlier Neolithic populations, which researchers read as suggesting stratification among the cultural groups. The admixture appears to have come from the mating of Western Steppe Herder males with Early European Farmer and Western Hunter-Gatherer females. The results supported the idea that the Battle Axe culture arose from migrations from southeast of the Baltic.

In the Early Bronze Age, copper was imported from Britain into Scandinavia in exchange for amber. This traded resource of the north was part of the exchange links that tied the Nordic Bronze Age to the British Isles.

Baltic amber beads were found in a foundational deposit under the large ziggurat of Aššur in Iraq, dated to about 1800-1750 BC. Archaeologists take this as showing that the Baltic and Mesopotamia were connected through long-distance contacts at that time.

philosophy.text: The Trundholm sun chariot is a Nordic Bronze Age artifact from Denmark. It is a bronze statue of a horse and a large bronze disk, set on a device with spoked wheels, and it represents the sun chariot.

The two sides of the Trundholm disk have been read as a sign of a belief about the Sun. By day the Sun was drawn from East to West with its bright side toward the Earth, and by night it returned from West to East showing its dark side.
It is thought that the Trundholm chariot was pulled around during religious rituals. The procession would have been a way to demonstrate the motion of the Sun in the heavens.

The Trundholm sun chariot from Denmark shows a horse and a large disc on spoked wheels. Its two sides have been read as a belief that the Sun crosses the sky from east to west by day and returns from west to east at night. It is thought to have been pulled around during religious rituals.

Evidence for horse-drawn chariots first appears in Scandinavia around 1700 BC. It takes the form of petroglyphs, chariot bits and whip handles, which shows the chariot was already a familiar idea before the sun chariot was made.

Some cultural similarities between the Nordic Bronze Age, the Sintashta/Andronovo culture and peoples of the Rigveda have been detected. The Nordic Bronze Age also kept close trade links with Mycenaean Greece, with whom it shares several striking similarities.
The Trundholm sculpture was discovered in 1902 in a peat bog on the Trundholm moor in Odsherred, in the northwestern part of Zealand. It was found with no accompanying objects.

The Egtved Girl was buried around 1370 BC in an oak coffin inside a barrow in Denmark. She lay on an ox hide, covered with a woollen blanket and a second ox hide, and the cremated remains of a child aged about five to six were placed at her feet. By the time she was excavated in 1921 most of her body had decomposed; only her hair, brain, teeth, nails and small traces of skin survived.
In 1998, archaeologists and metal detectorists returned to the original Trundholm site. They recovered 21 additional parts of the Sun Chariot, including wheels and spokes.
The Trundholm sun chariot is now in the collection of the National Museum of Denmark in Copenhagen. It is featured on the 1,000-krone banknote of the 2009 series.

culture.text: The Nordic Bronze Age kept close trade links with Mycenaean Greece, with whom it shares several striking similarities. Similarities have also been noted between its imagery and the Nebra Sky Disc from central Germany.

Scandinavia has left many thousands of rock carvings, known as petroglyphs, from the period 2500 to 500 BC. They are found most notably in western Sweden at Tanumshede and in Norway at Alta. Some carvings found in Bohuslän, dating from 800 to 500 BC, have themes of a sexual nature.

The Battle Axe culture, known from some 3,000 graves, made the battle axe a status symbol. Towards the end of the 3rd millennium BC its people, cattle herders with Steppe-derived ancestry, overran the Funnelbeaker people and advanced up to Uppland and the Oslofjord. They probably provided the language ancestral to the modern Scandinavian languages.

The Nordic Bronze Age culture emerged between 2000 and 1750 BC as a continuation of the Late Neolithic Dagger period. That period was rooted in the Battle Axe culture, the Single Grave Culture and the Bell Beaker culture, with added influence from Central Europe.
More Bronze Age swords have been found in Denmark than anywhere else in Europe. Uniform crucibles found at metal workshop sites indicate the mass production of certain metal artefacts.

Pitted Ware people were largely maritime hunters who traded with farming communities of the interior and with other hunter-gatherers of the Baltic Sea. Their culture lasted until about 2300 BC, when it was absorbed by the Battle Axe culture.

Burial customs in Scandinavia changed at the turn from the Older to the Younger Bronze Age. After a long period of inhumation, people gradually switched to cremation burials. During Period III (1300-1100 BCE), cremated remains were still buried in elongated pits or tree and oak coffins.

Early bronze artefacts in Scandinavia include hoards from Pile in Sweden and Skeldal in Denmark, dating from about 2000 to 1700 BC. Copper metallurgy had been practised earlier by the Bell Beaker culture in Jutland since about 2400 BC, producing axes and ornaments.

Pitted Ware graves held ceramics, boar tusks, pig jaws, and pendants of fox, dog and seal teeth. People of all ages and genders were buried in the same cemetery, with no indications of difference in social status.

The Battle Axe culture co-existed for a time with the hunter-gatherer Pitted Ware culture, which it eventually absorbed. It then developed into the Nordic Bronze Age, which has in turn been considered ancestral to the Germanic peoples.

Pitted Ware burials show complex customs, including mortuary houses and secondary burials. Cultural influences of the Battle Axe culture can be detected in these burials, though the two peoples do not appear to have mixed with each other.
